'''''Cephalanthera longifolia''''', the '''narrow-leaved helleborine''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''sword-leaved helleborine''' or '''long-leaved helleborine''', is a [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] in the family [[Orchidaceae]]. It is native to light woodland, and widespread across [[Europe]], [[Asia]] and [[North Africa]] from [[Ireland]] and [[Morocco]] to [[China]]. This includes the [[United Kingdom]], [[Iran]], [[Russia]], [[Kazakhstan]], [[Turkey]], [[Algeria]], [[India]], [[Pakistan]], [[Germany]], [[Italy]], [[France]], [[Spain]], [[Portugal]] and many other countries.<ref name="WCSP">[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=36658 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200028573 Flora of China, v 25 p 177, 头蕊兰 tou rui lan, ''Cephalanthera longifolia'' ]</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=cephalanthera+longifolia Altervista Flora Italiana, Cefalantera maggiore, Narrow Leaved Helleborine, ''Cephalanthera longifolia'' ]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Cephalanthera in Flora of Pakistan @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=106075 |access-date=2026-02-21 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref>

==Description==
''Cephalanthera longifolia'' reaches on average {{convert|20|-|60|cm}} in height in typical conditions. This orchid has erect and glabrous multiple stems. The leaves are dark green, long and narrowly tapering (hence the common name "sword-leaved helleborine"). The inflorescence is a lax, 5-20 flowered spike with the bell-shaped flowers ascending in an oblique spiral. The flowers are white, about {{convert|1|cm|1|abbr=on}} long, with a yellow-edged [[Labellum (botany)|labellum]] and they usually open only during the warmest and brightest hours of the day. This plant can be found in bloom from April to June, depending on location and altitude. The fruit is a dry capsule and the dust-like seed is dispersed by the wind.<ref name=NatureGate>{{cite web |url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/narrow-leaved-helleborine |title=Narrow-leaved Helleborine: ''Cephalanthera longifolia'' |publisher=NatureGate |access-date=2013-12-30}}</ref>

One unusual characteristic of this species is that some individuals are achlorophyllous (lacking green pigment) and take all their nutrition from [[mycorrhizal fungi]].<ref name="researchgate.net">[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228694257_Cephalanthera_longifolia_Neottieae_Orchidaceae_is_mixotrophic_A_comparative_study_between_green_and_nonphotosynthetic_individuals Canadian Journal of Botany - Cephalanthera longifolia is mixotrophic]</ref>

==Ecology==
The flowers are pollinated by solitary burrowing bees. The flowers produce little nectar and the yellowish dust on the labellum which the insects collect is of little nutritional value. The actual pollen is contained in  two pollinia which adhere to the hairs on the bee's back.<ref name=NatureGate/>

An investigation in Estonia determined that the [[mycorrhizal fungi|mycorrhizal partners]] of this orchid species include [[Thelephoraceae]] and [[Helotiales]].<ref name="researchgate.net"/> Another investigation indicated 9 mycorrhizal partners (still fewer than those recorded for ''[[Cephalanthera damasonium]]''): ''[[Bjerkandera adusta]]'', ''[[Phlebia acerina]]'', [[Sebacinaceae]], ''[[Tetracladium (fungus)|Tetracladium]] sp.'', and ''[[Tomentella]] sp''.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jse.12238 | doi=10.1111/jse.12238 | title=Fungal diversity and specificity in ''Cephalanthera damasonium'' and ''C. Longifolia'' (Orchidaceae) mycorrhizas | date=2017 | last1=Pecoraro | first1=Lorenzo | last2=Huang | first2=Laiqiang | last3=Caruso | first3=Tancredi | last4=Perotto | first4=Silvia | last5=Girlanda | first5=Mariangela | last6=Cai | first6=Lei | last7=Liu | first7=Zhong-Jian | journal=Journal of Systematics and Evolution | volume=55 | issue=2 | pages=158–169 | hdl=2318/1633076 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>

''Cephelanthera longifolia'' is vulnerable to grazing by deer.<ref>[https://wwt.sylva.org.uk/factsheet/43/Narrow-leaved%20Helleborine Woodland Wildlife Toolkit - Narrow-leaved helleborine]</ref><ref name=NatureGate/>

==Distribution==
''Cephalanthera longifolia'' is common in some parts of its European range, such as southern [[France]] and [[Spain]], but endangered particularly in northern areas such as [[Belgium]]. In [[Great Britain|Britain]] and [[Ireland]] it is a quite uncommon and declining species, and conservation work is being carried out at a number of sites to safeguard it (see also [[Galley Down Wood]]). In 2007 it was listed as a priority species under the UK Biodiversity Action Plan. The charity [[Plantlife International]] is leading this work in the [[United Kingdom]].

==Habitat==
Sword-leaved helleborine usually grows in damp woodland places (mainly oak and beech), forest edges and rocky slopes.<ref name=NatureGate/> These plants prefer calcareous soils and in well exposed places, at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|1400|m}} above sea level.

This species was once abundant, when forests were used for grazing livestock and trees were coppiced, but is now threatened by overgrowth of larger plants. As the flower spikes are eaten by deer, the sword-leaved helleborine is also threatened by the increase of deer populations following extirpation of large predators like the wolf and brown bear in many parts of Europe.<ref name=NatureGate/>

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Cephalanthera'' comes from the Greek κεφαλή ''kephalē'' (head) and ἄνθηρα ''anthēra'' ([[anther]]): the anther is placed at the top (head) of the [[Column (botany)|column]].<ref name=Gilb55>{{Cite book |last1=Gilbert-Carter |first1=H. |date=1955 |title=Glossary of the British Flora |publisher=Cambridge University Press |oclc=867791719 |page=19 }}</ref> The Latin name ''longifolia '' means ''with long leaves ''.

"Helleborine" may refer to deer using the orchid for food (many conservationists have noted that helleborine orchids are grazed by deer<ref>[https://www.plantlife.org.uk/application/files/4914/7913/4059/Epipactis_youngiana_species_dossier.pdf Plantlife - Epipactis youngiana]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/wfsoc/wfs_reports/2001/2001_watlington_hill_11_july_report.htm |title=Wildflower Society Online Report |access-date=2018-12-06 |archive-date=2018-12-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181206192538/https://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/wfsoc/wfs_reports/2001/2001_watlington_hill_11_july_report.htm }}</ref><ref>[http://kammekat.tripod.com/ceplongifoliaen.htm Finnish Orchids]</ref>). Alternatively it may denote that the plants are similar to [[hellebores]] (a group of species in the family [[Ranunculaceae]]). "Hellebore" comes from the Greek "álkē" and "bora", translating as "fawn" and "food of beasts".<ref>[https://www.dictionary.com/browse/hellebore Dictionary.com]</ref>
